title: On-chip optical isolators
authors: Abanoub Mikhail, Nikolay Solodovchenko, Sen Xu, Fan Zhang, Maksim Tumashov, Mingzhao Song, Sergei Makarov, Andrey Bogdanov
abstract: Optical isolation suppresses back-reflections that destabilize lasers, produce parasitic interference, and increase crosstalk in photonic systems. Although free-space and fibre-optic isolators are mature, no broadly adopted on-chip technology yet combines strong isolation, low insertion loss, broad bandwidth, compact footprint, and scalable fabrication. The difficulty is twofold: Lorentz reciprocity must be broken, and every relevant backward spatial, spectral, and polarization channel must be suppressed. This Review develops a common framework for assessing proposed solutions. We first distinguish pairwise nonreciprocity from intensity-asymmetric transmission and from true isolation using the constitutive relations and scattering matrix. We then compare three physical routes to an integrated nonreciprocal response: magneto-optical bias, externally driven space-time modulation, and nonlinear optical processes. Topological and non-Hermitian systems are treated as cross-cutting design frameworks that can route, protect, or enhance an underlying nonreciprocal response, but do not by themselves break reciprocity. Finally, we examine fundamental constraints and practical trade-offs among isolation, insertion loss, bandwidth, footprint, modal coverage, drive requirements, and fabrication compatibility. The resulting mechanism-based perspective connects reciprocity-breaking physics to the requirements of scalable photonic integrated circuits.
summary: This review provides a comprehensive, mechanism-based framework for achieving optical isolation on photonic chips. It systematically compares three physical methods—magneto-optics, time modulation, and nonlinearity—to break Lorentz reciprocity. The paper is crucial for guiding the development of next-generation, high-performance integrated quantum optical circuits.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a scalable, on-chip optical isolator that combines strong nonreciprocal isolation with low insertion loss and broad bandwidth.
main_result: The review establishes a common framework by classifying three primary physical routes—magneto-optical bias, external space-time modulation, and nonlinear processes—for breaking Lorentz reciprocity in integrated photonics.
method: The analysis uses the scattering matrix formalism and develops a mechanism-based perspective to distinguish true isolation from mere intensity asymmetry.
model_or_system: The focus is on Photonic Integrated Circuits (PICs) containing lasers and optical components, modeled using electromagnetic theory and analyzed via the scattering matrix ($\mathbf{S}$).

important_parameters: Lorentz reciprocity breaking mechanisms (magnetization, time-varying fields, nonlinearity), and practical trade-offs like footprint and drive requirements.
main_assumptions: The review assumes the applicability of linear/time-invariant electromagnetic theory while discussing extensions using non-Hermitian and topological concepts.

paper_structure: The paper first clarifies the physical requirements for isolation, then systematically distinguishes between different types of nonreciprocity, and finally compares the three main physical mechanisms (MO, Space-time, Nonlinear) before discussing advanced frameworks.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it bridges fundamental symmetry-breaking physics (Lorentz reciprocity) directly to the engineering requirements of advanced quantum optical components like integrated lasers and quantum light sources.

An optical isolator is characterized by a nonreciprocal scattering matrix and strong suppression of transmission in one direction while maintaining high transmission in the opposite direction. An optical diode exhibits direction-dependent transmission, although the degree and origin of the asymmetry may depend on the operating conditions.
